title: Basic Types
subtitle: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, any, unknown, void, never
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JavaScript has 8 primitive types but no way to enforce which type a variable holds. TypeScript maps these to named types you can annotate and the compiler enforces.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript's basic types mirror JavaScript's primitives: string, number, boolean, null, undefined. Plus TypeScript-specific helpers: any (opt-out of type checking), unknown (safe any), void (no return value), never (impossible value).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Everywhere. These are the building blocks of every TypeScript program.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid any — it turns off type checking. Use unknown instead when you genuinely don't know the type. Prefer explicit types for function parameters; let inference handle variable declarations.

explainModes.beginner: TypeScript has named versions of JavaScript's types: string for text, number for numbers, boolean for true/false. It also has any (means 'anything goes, no checking') and unknown (safer version — you must check the type before using it). void means a function returns nothing. never means something can never happen.
explainModes.simple: string, number, boolean — basic primitives. null and undefined — their own types (with strictNullChecks). any — disables type checking (avoid). unknown — like any but safe; must narrow before use. void — function return type when no value returned. never — return type of functions that throw or never return (infinite loop). object — non-primitive. Function — typed with parameter and return types.
explainModes.standard: strictNullChecks (enabled with strict): null and undefined are NOT assignable to other types — prevents a whole class of bugs. Without it, null is assignable to string (like Java's null). With it: let x: string = null is an error. Use string | null for nullable strings. The undefined type is for uninitialized or missing values. Use type: type | undefined for optional values.
explainModes.technical: number covers both integers and floats (IEEE 754 double precision — same as JS). bigint for arbitrary precision integers (64-bit+). symbol for unique identifiers. Template literal types: type Greeting = `Hello, ${string}` — a string that starts with 'Hello, '. Literal types: type Direction = 'left' | 'right' — only those exact values allowed. const assertion: const config = { port: 3000 } as const — port has type 3000 (literal), not number.
explainModes.deepDive: The never type represents the bottom type — a value that can never exist. Use case: exhaustive checks. if (x is string) ... else if (x is number) ... else { const _check: never = x } — if x has no remaining type variants, the assignment to never compiles; if you later add a new union member and forget to handle it, it errors. This pattern enforces exhaustive switch/if handling at compile time. satisfies operator (TS 4.9): const config = { port: 3000 } satisfies Config — validates against Config but keeps the literal type (3000, not number).

questions.question: What is the difference between any and unknown?
options: They are identical — any is just an alias for unknown
any allows using the value without type checks; unknown requires narrowing first
any is for primitives, unknown is for objects
questions.explanation: Both accept any value, but unknown is safer. With any, you can call methods and access properties without checks — risky because the type might be wrong at runtime. With unknown, TypeScript forces you to narrow the type first (typeof check, instanceof, etc.) before using it. Always prefer unknown over any when you're unsure of the type.

faq.a: With strictNullChecks (on by default with strict: true), null and undefined are their own types — they can't be assigned to string, number, etc. This prevents a huge category of 'Cannot read property of null' runtime errors. To allow null: use string | null. This is the single most impactful TypeScript setting.

examples: function parseJSON(input: string): unknown — return unknown, force callers to narrow
type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'closed' — literal union instead of string
function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error() } — exhaustive check helper
